card.hook: Picture a Scottish-French castle parked in the middle of the Rockies, with white water rushing past in front of it. That's the view from the river bank, and it's quieter than the roadside lookout.
card.stand_here: Stand at Bow Falls, on the east side of the falls. Face upstream over the rapids and the hotel will be to the south, rising in the distance beyond the water. Walk along the bank for a minute until you find a clear line between the rapids and the towers.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the rapids and the hotel fit together. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer. Zoom 0.5x is fun for a close shot of the rushing water, but the hotel will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the rapids in the lower third and the hotel roofs on one of the upper lines, then tap the hotel and slide it a little darker so the pale stone and bright water don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the day usually means fewer people on the bank. The pale stone and pointed roofs stand out nicely against the forested slopes behind.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Lookout Patio on the hotel's own grounds, the terrace on the hotel side, which one guide calls Banff's best patio for panoramic Rockies views. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x with the hotel over your shoulder, and check it's actually in the shot before you smile. Bad weather? The grand staircases at either end of the main lobby are great for walking-toward-the-camera shots.
card.ask_someone: For the classic whole-hotel view, ask a passer-by to stand on the platform by the barricade at the corner of Buffalo Street and Tunnel Mountain Road (Surprise Corner), so the hotel shows above the trees across the valley.
card.rules_and_safety: At Surprise Corner the cliff edge is covered in loose gravel and a fall would be perilous, so stay well back. Bow Falls is a public park area inside Banff National Park, so check the Parks Canada site for any pass requirements, and the hotel's own site for anything inside the building.
card.challenge: Get the rapids, the towers and one pointed copper roof all in one shot, with the water nice and level. Bonus points if you keep your shoes dry.
card.good_to_know: The hotel opened in 1888 as one of Canada's early grand railway hotels, built by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The original wooden building burned down in 1926, so what you see now is mostly the 1914 centre tower with the 1927 and 1928 wings either side, built in Rundle limestone. The buildings became a National Historic Site of Canada in 1988.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Bow Falls, on the east side of the falls. Face upstream over the rapids and the hotel will be to the south, rising in the distance beyond the water. Walk along the bank for a minute until you find a clear line between the rapids and the towers.

card.hook: Picture a little cabin gliding up its cable with nothing but open sky around it. That's the shot here, and it's worth waiting a minute for.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map. It sits right at the Banff Gondola, so there's no extra walk. Face the building, then take a few steps back or to one side until nothing blocks your view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the building and the cabins together. Go to 0.5x if you want more sky and scenery, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a single cabin on the cable.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the horizon and the building's edges up with them, so the whole picture looks calm and straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you soft light, and a day with some clear sky helps a lot. Midday sun bounces off the glass and metal, so it can look harsh.
card.selfie_here: If you ride up, try the lookout platform beside the upper terminal at the summit. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and tuck the mountain views in behind you. The wooden boardwalk toward Sanson's Peak is also named as a good photo area, with wide views behind you.
card.ask_someone: At the lower terminal, ask your photographer to stand well back from the base building so the cable rising up the mountain fits in the frame, with you standing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Bears sometimes show up along Banff roads. If there's a bear jam, one local guide says to stay in your car, keep your distance, and never take a selfie with a bear. Check the official site for current access information before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a cabin in a clear patch of sky, then take a second shot with you grinning in the corner and the cabin 'hanging' over your head.
card.good_to_know: The Banff Gondola is a gondola lift, and it's the second stop on this map. The building and the cabins on their cable make a clear subject, so even a quick snap shows where you are. The views from the top are a whole separate set of photos if you decide to ride.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map. It sits right at the Banff Gondola, so there's no extra walk. Face the building, then take a few steps back or to one side until nothing blocks your view.

card.hook: Here's the twist: the best photo of Mount Norquay is the one where you turn your back on it. Face the other way and the whole Bow Valley opens up below you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the roadside pullout with the grassy slope (the 'Green Spot') on Mount Norquay Road, on the right about 4.8 km up the road from town, below the cement barrier. Face out over Banff townsite and Mount Rundle, with Norquay behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the town, the valley and Rundle together. Go to 0.5x for more of the grassy slope in front, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Rundle's ridge or to snap sheep from far away.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the town, then nudge it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour near sunset.
card.best_time: Afternoon through to sunset is the sweet spot. One guide also suggests sunrise.
card.selfie_here: Try the Green Spot itself, on the grassy slope by the stone retaining wall (pull over and walk onto the grass, where the Parks Canada red chairs sit). Use the front camera, go to 0.5x, and hold your phone low so the wide Banff view fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep a safe distance from any bighorn sheep. Parking can be full, and the road may be icy in winter. If you want the Banff sign selfie, use the new spot by the train station, not the busy roadside, and check it's still there.
card.challenge: Get a patch of grass, the town and Rundle's ridge all in one shot, with bonus points if a bighorn photobombs from a respectful distance.
card.good_to_know: Mount Norquay was named in 1904 after John Norquay, premier of Manitoba from 1878 to 1887. The ski area opened its lodge in 1929. In 1948 it became the second in Canada to install a chairlift, and in summer the North American chairlift runs for sightseeing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the roadside pullout with the grassy slope (the 'Green Spot') on Mount Norquay Road, on the right about 4.8 km up the road from town, below the cement barrier. Face out over Banff townsite and Mount Rundle, with Norquay behind you.

card.hook: Most people photograph hot springs from the water and end up with a close-up of steam and heads. Walk up the trail instead, and the whole place spreads out below you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Sulphur Mountain Trail, a short way up the trail above the springs. The springs lie to the west, so face down over the bathhouse buildings and pools toward the surrounding peaks.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole scene: buildings, pools and mountains. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pools and the peak shapes. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and slope, and keep the buildings away from the edges, where they stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pools or buildings, then drag the slider to make the shot a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the steam doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day the light is softer and flatters both the mountains and the buildings. Cooler air tends to show more steam over the pools.
card.selfie_here: On the Sulphur Mountain trail a short way up from the springs, use the front camera at 0.5x with the springs below and the peaks over your shoulder. For a classic shot inside the paid area, stand at the pool edge on the deck with the water behind you, facing Mount Rundle.
card.ask_someone: On the wide terrace in front of the bathhouse, ask a passer-by to shoot you with the pool and building in frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One travel blog says drones and selfie sticks aren't allowed here, so check the official site before you go. The pool area is paid, and opening status can vary, so confirm before you visit. Keep your phone away from wet hands and steam, and wipe the camera glass before each shot, because a misted one makes everything look soft.
card.challenge: Put the buildings and pools in the bottom third, tuck a bit of trail or trees into the corner, and see if you can make the whole valley look like a tiny model village.
card.good_to_know: The water is kept at about 38 °C, the hottest of the Banff springs. At 1,585 metres, this is the highest hot spring in Canada. The Stoney Nakoda and Secwépemc used the springs long before Europeans arrived in 1883, and the bathhouse became a Registered Federal Heritage Building in 1931.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Sulphur Mountain Trail, a short way up the trail above the springs. The springs lie to the west, so face down over the bathhouse buildings and pools toward the surrounding peaks.

card.hook: Here's a funny secret: the most famous view near Bow Falls is really a hotel postcard, and the water is the bonus. The falls are fairly small, but they fit the river, white water and mountains into one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on Surprise Corner, the elevated platform above the falls off Tunnel Mountain Road. Face the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel rising above the trees, with the Spray Valley beyond.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the hotel above the trees. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the water below. Zoom 0.5x shows more of the valley, but the falls will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the falls, then slide it a little darker so the white water keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights Sulphur Mountain. In the afternoon the sun sets over the hotel, so you get more backlight. Midday in summer is when the coach-tour crowds peak.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge over the Bow River near Bow Falls. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the river and mountain over your shoulder. The falls themselves won't be behind you here.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the south side viewing area, where photographers frame the falls with the Fairmont Banff Springs hotel in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are not allowed here. The upper clifftop viewpoint is reported closed in winter and paths can be icy, so check the official site before you go. Give your phone's camera a wipe first, as spray can leave marks.
card.challenge: Take the hotel shot at zoom 1x, 2x and 5x, then pick your winner and tell whoever's with you why it's the best.
card.good_to_know: Bow Falls tumbles down the Bow River just before it meets the Spray River. It's an easy walk from Banff, which is why so many visitors come. You might also know it from the 1953 film River of No Return with Marilyn Monroe.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Surprise Corner, the elevated platform above the falls off Tunnel Mountain Road. Face the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel rising above the trees, with the Spray Valley beyond.

card.hook: Picture a dock poking out into glassy water, a huge mountain doubled in the surface, and not a ripple in sight. That's Mount Rundle on a still morning at the Second Vermilion Lake, and yes, it looks as good as it sounds.
card.stand_here: Head to the shoreline and dock at the Second Vermilion Lake, on Vermilion Lakes Road. Face across the water to Mount Rundle, with the dock or boardwalk in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view of Rundle and its reflection. Try 0.5x if you want the dock to fill the bottom of the picture, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to zoom in on the peak and its mirror image.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, so the mountain and sky get most of the frame, with the dock leading the eye in.
card.best_time: Aim for about 30 minutes before sunrise, when the lake is calm and Rundle catches the first light. If the water is rippled, wait a minute for a calm moment and the reflection will come back.
card.selfie_here: Walk out onto the first dock you reach on Vermilion Lakes Road when coming from the highway. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep Mount Rundle rising behind your shoulder. If you'd rather have a higher view, the Vermilion Lakes Viewpoint pull-out gives you the lake chain below with Rundle in the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the small dock and boardwalk at the shore of the Second Vermilion Lake, while you stand in front of them, so the whole lake and Mount Rundle fit in the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: The road is popular with cyclists, so stay off the carriageway while you shoot. Moose and elk can be around, so keep your distance, and expect plenty of mosquitoes in summer. A park pass is probably needed at some times of year, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots: a wide one with dock, water and mountain, then a tight one of just the peak and its reflection, and see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: The Vermilion Lakes are a chain of three lakes just west of Banff, in the Bow River valley at the foot of Mount Norquay. They sit between the Trans-Canada Highway and the railway tracks, so they're easy to reach from town. They're also old: there's evidence of people camping and making obsidian tools here about 10,800 years ago.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the shoreline and dock at the Second Vermilion Lake, on Vermilion Lakes Road. Face across the water to Mount Rundle, with the dock or boardwalk in front of you.

card.hook: Picture steam curling off warm water while cold mountain air nips at your nose, and the Rocky peaks just standing there behind it. That's the free show at Cave and Basin, the spot where Banff National Park began.
card.stand_here: Head for the front of the outdoor basin, inside the historic building's grounds, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the steaming water with the Rocky Mountain peaks rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole basin and the mountains in one frame, then go to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks or the rising steam.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the steam, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white vapour keeps its detail and the sky stays rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Steam tends to show best on cold days, so a chilly morning is your best bet.
card.selfie_here: Climb the short stairs on your right as you near the entrance to the viewing deck above the buildings, which looks over the basin toward Mount Cory, Mount Norquay and Cascade Mountain. For another fun option, look for one of the Parks Canada red chairs on the grounds. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a bit higher and check the screen to see what's over your shoulder before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Near the gift shop in the admission area, just before the short walk to the main building, ask a passer-by to take your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the marked paths and boardwalks, because the springs are home to the endangered Banff Springs snail. If you go into the cave, remember to duck as you enter (that's from a visitor's review). The cave is inside the admission building, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on Live Photo and catch the steam drifting past the mountains, then see if you can get the water's edge sitting on the lower gridline too.
card.good_to_know: In 1883 three railway workers lowered themselves through a hole in the cave roof using a felled tree. By 1885 the Canadian government had reserved about 26 square kilometres around the springs, which was the start of Canada's national parks. The site became a National Historic Site in 1981.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the front of the outdoor basin, inside the historic building's grounds, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the steaming water with the Rocky Mountain peaks rising behind it.

card.hook: Picture a main street where every shopfront seems to be pointing at a mountain. That's Banff Avenue, and Cascade Mountain sits right at the end of it like it was put there on purpose.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Cascade of Time Garden, near the south end of Banff Avenue on the south side of the Bow River. Face back north, so the flower beds and pools are in front of you and the avenue and Cascade Mountain rise behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit flowers, street and mountain in one shot. Then try zoom 2x for a tighter view of the peak, or zoom 0.5x close to the flowers for a bigger splash of foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the avenue running straight up the middle, and leave a little sky above the peak.
card.best_time: Late spring through summer, when the flowers are in bloom. That's when the garden gives you its softest, greenest version of the street view.
card.selfie_here: Try the painted centre divider in the middle of Banff Avenue, with Cascade Mountain at the far end of the street. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the mountain over your shoulder. This spot is approximate, so play with the angle.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Banff Avenue bridge at the south end and shoot back up the avenue, while you pose up the street on the pavement or median so you and Cascade Mountain both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Cars use both sides of Banff Avenue, so keep to the pavement or median and don't step into the road for a better angle. Gardens and bridges can have seasonal works, so check locally before you go.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the street runs dead straight to the mountain, with nobody's head poking into the line. Bonus points if the flowers look like they're in on it.
card.good_to_know: Banff Avenue is a busy through-street that runs straight towards Cascade Mountain. That tidy line is why the view works so well on a phone. The Cascade of Time Garden is free to visit and easy to reach on foot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Cascade of Time Garden, near the south end of Banff Avenue on the south side of the Bow River. Face back north, so the flower beds and pools are in front of you and the avenue and Cascade Mountain rise behind them.

card.hook: Mount Rundle looks like a giant layered cake that someone tipped sideways, and that tilt is exactly why your photo will look good. Those diagonal rock bands do half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Head for the shoreline of the second lake at Vermilion Lakes, just off Vermilion Lakes Road west of town. From the spot on the map, Mount Rundle is about 66 m to the south, about 1 minute on foot, so face south and look up.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the slopes. Go to 0.5x for more sky and the full sweep of the rock bands, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single cliff or ridge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the line where the cliffs meet the tree-covered slopes, and let the tilted rock bands run diagonally across the frame.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset is your best bet for warm colour, so check the sunset time for the day you visit. Mornings are deep shadow, which is moodier but darker.
card.selfie_here: Try the first of the three docks along Vermilion Lakes Road, west of Banff, which has views of Rundle over the lakes. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and try to get the mountain over your shoulder (check the angle when you arrive). Surprise Corner on Tunnel Mountain Road is another good one, with the Fairmont Banff Springs in front and Rundle rising behind.
card.ask_someone: For the classic shot, ask a passer-by at the pull-off at the end of Vermilion Lakes Road to snap you with the lakes in the foreground and Rundle filling the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Mount Rundle is in Banff National Park, so check the official Parks Canada site before you go for any park pass or access rules.
card.challenge: Find the steepest diagonal in the rock and make it run corner to corner in your frame, like a giant staircase for mountain goats.
card.good_to_know: Rundle is less a single peak than a small range, stretching over 12 kilometres with seven distinct peaks. The highest is the third peak southeast of Banff, at 2,949 metres. John Palliser named it in 1858 after the Reverend Robert Rundle, a Methodist missionary, and the painter Walter Phillips called it his "bread and butter mountain" because its mood and colour kept changing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the shoreline of the second lake at Vermilion Lakes, just off Vermilion Lakes Road west of town. From the spot on the map, Mount Rundle is about 66 m to the south, about 1 minute on foot, so face south and look up.

card.hook: Surprise Corner has a sneaky secret: the obvious platform isn't the best spot. Walk a few minutes further and the grand hotel looks even better.
card.stand_here: Stand at the barricade and small pedestrian area by the cliff edge, a short way up Tunnel Mountain Road past the Surprise Corner parking lot. Face the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, with Spray Valley around it and Sulphur Mountain behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the hotel, the valley and Sulphur Mountain in one shot. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the hotel closer and cut out empty sky. Save zoom 0.5x for a sweeping valley view, because the hotel will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the hotel on one of the crossing points instead of dead centre, with treetops filling the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the hotel and mountain. Take a quick test shot to check how it looks.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at the barricade area on Tunnel Mountain Road, or on the platform if it's open. Turn so the hotel sits over your shoulder, and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of it in.
card.ask_someone: If the platform is open, ask someone to stand by the small parking lot at the corner of Buffalo Street and Tunnel Mountain Road and face the platform and stairs across the road, while you stand up on the platform.
card.rules_and_safety: The cliff edge is loose and dangerous, so stay behind the barricade and rest your phone against it rather than leaning out. Stay on the trail and don't walk on the cliffs.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the hotel pokes out of the treetops like it's playing hide-and-seek, then one where you're doing the same thing.
card.good_to_know: The hotel sits above the treetops with Sulphur Mountain rising behind it, but you can't see the Bow River from the raised platform. The parking lot is very small and fills quickly. The platform was reported closed for maintenance in late September 2025, so check before you count on it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the barricade and small pedestrian area by the cliff edge, a short way up Tunnel Mountain Road past the Surprise Corner parking lot. Face the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, with Spray Valley around it and Sulphur Mountain behind.

card.hook: Walk down Banff Avenue and the shop fronts start to blur together, then you hit a log-built museum with a wooden veranda that looks like it wandered in from another century. It's an easy, friendly first stop, and the logs do most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Banff Avenue on the west sidewalk, near the museum's historical marker, and face north. The log front sits right there with the street leading your eye past it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole log front in from the sidewalk. If traffic or people push you in close, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the log framing and the veranda.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the building on one side of the frame and let the street fill the other, and keep your phone upright and level so the log walls stay straight.
card.best_time: There's no special best time for this one, and the street may be busy at any hour. Take a few frames in a row and pick the one where nobody's walking through.
card.selfie_here: Try the sidewalk in front of the museum's entrance at 91 Banff Avenue, which one listing calls one of the best selfie places in town. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the museum over your shoulder, and be ready to queue.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the public sidewalk. If you want to go inside or onto the grounds, check the official site first, as access and photo rules there may differ.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the veranda and entrance sign with not a single stranger in it, and give yourself bonus points for dead-straight log walls.
card.good_to_know: The museum's collection began in 1895, and the building went up in 1903, designed by John Stocks, an engineer working for the territorial government. It's the oldest building looked after by Parks Canada and became a National Historic Site in 1985. Inside are about 5,000 specimens of animals, plants and minerals from the area, and the logs were restored in 2010 with a clear coating, which is why they look so warm in photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Banff Avenue on the west sidewalk, near the museum's historical marker, and face north. The log front sits right there with the street leading your eye past it.
